title: Malachi 2:1–9
context: The LORD of Armies continues to address the priests with a commandment and a warning: if they will not give glory to his name, he will curse their blessings and disgrace them (2:1–3). He recalls his covenant with Levi, a covenant of life and peace, when the priest revered God, taught true instruction, and turned many from iniquity (2:4–7; compare Numbers 25:12–13 and Deuteronomy 33:8–11). The present priests have turned aside, caused many to stumble, and shown partiality, so the LORD has made them contemptible (2:8–9). In 2:3, the word rendered “offspring” can also be rendered “seed.”

verses.text: “Now, you priests, this commandment is for you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now, you priests, this commandment is for you.” Arminian readers see the LORD addressing the priests directly, holding leaders accountable for their teaching and worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priests singled out for warning. Shared ground: those who lead God’s people in worship bear special responsibility to honor his name.

verses.text: If you will not listen, and if you will not take it to heart, to give glory to my name,” says the LORD of Armies, “then I will send the curse on you, and I will curse your blessings. Indeed, I have cursed them already, because you do not take it to heart.
verses.arminianNotes: “If you will not listen, and if you will not take it to heart,” and “I will curse your blessings.” Arminian readers see a conditional warning that calls the priests to respond while there is time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the warning as real and urgent. The LORD adds, “I have cursed them already,” and readers in this tradition see judgment already under way for those who will not take his word to heart.

verses.text: Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and will spread dung on your faces, even the dung of your feasts; and you will be taken away with it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I will rebuke your offspring, and will spread dung on your faces.” Arminian readers see a shocking image of disgrace for priests who despised the LORD’s table.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see humiliation matched to contempt. The word rendered “offspring” can also be rendered “seed,” and readers in this tradition hold both senses as possible.

verses.text: You will know that I have sent this commandment to you, that my covenant may be with Levi,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “You will know that I have sent this commandment to you, that my covenant may be with Levi.” Arminian readers see the warning aimed at restoring the priests to the covenant ideal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the purpose of the warning as renewal of the covenant with Levi. Readers in this tradition connect this with passages such as Numbers 25:12–13 and Deuteronomy 33:8–11, cited by reference.

verses.text: “My covenant was with him of life and peace; and I gave them to him that he might be reverent toward me; and he was reverent toward me, and stood in awe of my name.
verses.arminianNotes: “My covenant was with him of life and peace,” and “he was reverent toward me, and stood in awe of my name.” Arminian readers see the faithful priesthood of the past held up as a model.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant of life and peace given to Levi. Shared ground: reverence for God’s name is at the heart of faithful ministry, in contrast to the contempt of 1:6.

verses.text: The law of truth was in his mouth, and unrighteousness was not found in his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and turned many away from iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: “The law of truth was in his mouth, and unrighteousness was not found in his lips.” Arminian readers see faithful teaching and upright living that “turned many away from iniquity.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the ideal priest as both teacher and example. Readers in this tradition note that true ministry leads others to turn from sin, not merely to perform rituals.

verses.text: For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth; for he is the messenger of the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth; for he is the messenger of the LORD of Armies.” Arminian readers see the priest’s role as teacher of God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priest as “the messenger of the LORD,” a striking title. Readers in this tradition note the link with the name Malachi, “my messenger,” and with the messenger of 3:1, cited by reference.

verses.text: But you have turned away from the path. You have caused many to stumble in the law. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “But you have turned away from the path. You have caused many to stumble in the law.” Arminian readers see the priests’ failure harming others, the opposite of Levi’s example in 2:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see corrupted teaching leading many astray. Shared ground: leaders who misuse God’s law do double harm, falling themselves and causing others to stumble.

verses.text: “Therefore I have also made you contemptible and wicked before all the people, according to the way you have not kept my ways, but have had respect for persons in the law.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I have also made you contemptible and wicked before all the people.” Arminian readers see the priests who despised God now despised by the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a fitting judgment. Readers in this tradition note the charge of “respect for persons in the law,” partiality that corrupts justice and teaching alike.
